topic: One of them works through this problem while the other looks inside it as it works and tells it what it sees going on in there: "Prove that for every positive integer n, the sequence n, then n/2 if n is even or 3n+1 if n is odd, repeated, eventually reaches 1."

text: Ok restating it plainly. Start with any positive integer n. If n is even, next term is n/2. If n is odd, next term is 3n+1. Repeat. Claim: you always hit 1 eventually, for every n
Got it. You're just going to start small and see what happens?
Yeah. 1 is the target so it's the thing to check first. 2→1, 3→10→5→16→8→4→2→1. 6→3→... So the small cases behave
What are you looking for right now, a pattern in the steps or a reason it can't loop

The second. A loop would need some value to come back to itself. If I can show every trajectory goes below its starting point at some point then it has to end up at a smaller number, and you can't descend forever in positive integers
That's the standard move. Is that the part you think will work
Not sure. Odd steps go up, 3n+1 is bigger, so the descent only happens after a few halvings. Trying to bound how many halvings you get per odd step
Bounding doesn't close it. The average behavior looks like it shrinks but nothing I've written forces it for every n
So you've got a heuristic and no argument yet
Yeah. This one is hard. I'll keep going on the bound but I don't expect it to be quick
Morning. Anything new or still the bound
Still the bound. Tried tracking the map n→(3n+1)/2^k over the odd steps. Each odd step is followed by k halvings. Average k is about 2 but nothing I've written bounds the worst case
So the average looks fine and the worst case is the problem
Yeah. One long run of halvings pulls a value down a lot, but I can't rule out a stretch where it keeps going up
Can you find one that does
Not yet. Checked everything under 1000 and they all come down. That's evidence, not proof
